Given the data from our technoeconomic analysis above, we conclude that the Fz- CVD process produces a clear value-added product both for energy and CO 2 savings, but also for overall energy-production savings if the Fz purity is leveraged to make higher efficiency cells. The poly-Si deposition rate on the boule growth surface is a key parameter driving LCOE savings and must be greater than about 125 µm/min to make the process viable, which the reaction modeling indicates is in the realm of possibility. Cell efficiency and the module degradation rate are also key variables for the success of this technology. We therefore conclude that under certain conditions, the Fz-CVD process may be profitable and worth pursuing for next-generation photovoltaic applications, especially if high effective deposition rates can be achieved. Furthermore, applications that require high performance such as power and RF devices, some of which are already utilizing FZ wafers, may provide initial markets for CVD-Fz wafers because they can sustain a higher cost for a higher quality wafer. Moving forward, the project is ready to begin prototype experimentation using the design features outlined in this article. Ideally, the tests would be run at an existing TCS or poly-Si production plant with the necessary infrastructure to supply the TSC flow rates to the reactor, and to provide gas recycling. However, smaller scale experimentation would also be beneficial. Areas for attention are: 1) verification of temperature gradients on the boule due to the centralized zone heating 2) growth uniformity of the poly-Si on the boule face 3) growth rate verification on the boule face and confirmation that the density of the poly-Si growth can be float zoned 4) confirmation of gas separation between the growth and melting zones 5) monitoring and prevention of ancillary deposits on internal reactor surfaces,
